newsitem.title: USA: Car airbag depowering seen a trade off in lives.
newsitem.headline: Car airbag depowering seen a trade off in lives.

text.p: The recent proposal to reduce the power of airbags was based on a study's estimate that it would save over 600 lives of people wearing seatbelts, though depowered bags would cost the lives of 2,000 unbelted people a year, U.S. officials said Tuesday.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) said it based its proposal to depower airbags on Australian tests on General Motors -designed Holden cars that showed lower-powered bags better protected restrained adults.
It estimated that if bags on U.S. cars were depowered, 643 lives could be saved annually, although up to 2,000 unbelted occupants could be killed.

While the bags are credited with saving about 1,700 lives since introduced in the 1980s, their 200-mile-an-hour inflating force has been blamed for the deaths of 32 children and some 20 adults, many of them women or frail older people.

But the NHTSA and safety advocates have emphasized that airbags are only a supplementary safety device, and that seat belts are the most effective protective measure. They add that all states except New Hampshire require seat belt use.
U.S. airbag standards were set when most occupants did not wear seat belts, but now 68 percent do. Those who where seatbelts are better protected by the airbag, experts say.
Safety experts say it was no longer logical for the United States to base airbag safety on occupants riding without seat belts when the majority now use them.
They add that occupants not obeying seat belt laws should not be protected by high-power airbags that put children and small and frail adults at risk.

The NHTSA proposal to depower bags by 20-35 percent is to go into effect next month, along with another proposal to allow car owners to have mechanics disconnect their bags if they consider them an unacceptable safety risk.
